course.title: Blood Culture Sampling
course.splitRationale: The source names its own two sections and the split holds: slides 4-16 are 'what a blood culture is and what a good one requires', slides 17-39 are 'how you actually take one and what you are accountable for'. That is a shift from knowing to doing, and each half runs about 12 minutes of narration - comfortably inside one sitting. Each section ships as its own SCORM package with its own welcome, objectives and results slide, as this studio does.
course.learningTimeNote: Indicative seat time to work through the module once, attentively: narration at 140 words per minute, plus 6s per panel the learner opens, plus per-question time for each knowledge check, plus a 10% allowance for pauses, replays and navigation. On-screen text is not counted separately because it is revealed in step with the narration that explains it.

smeQueries.issue: The recommended adult blood volume is given two different ways. Slide 12 states 8-10 mL per bottle. Slide 22 states 20-30 mL per set, typically 10 mL in each bottle - which implies either a third bottle or 10-15 mL per bottle. The storyboard teaches 8-10 mL per bottle throughout, from slide 12. Please confirm the figure to teach, as this is the single most important determinant of culture yield and learners will be audited against it.
A text box reading 'Abnormal muscle function' appears on nine slides. Treated as leftover text from the deck this template was cloned from, and excluded. Please confirm it is not intended content.

The course menu and the Section 1 contents slide both list 'Common Bloodstream Pathogens' as a Section 1 topic, but the organisms slide sits at slide 31, inside Section 2. The storyboard places it at the end of Section 1, following the menu. Please confirm.

'Before starting antibiotics' appears in the indications list on slide 8, but it is a timing rule rather than an indication - the same point is made properly on slide 9. It has been kept in both places. Please confirm, or let us drop it from the indications list.

Two text problems in the source: the heading on slide 20 reads 'Proecdure', and the body placeholder on slide 16 repeats 'Order of Draw' twice. Both corrected silently. Flagging in case either signals missing content.

Slide 14 lists chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine and isopropyl alcohol as options with chlorhexidine preferred in adults; slide 21 instructs chlorhexidine specifically. Please confirm whether the procedure mandates chlorhexidine or allows the alternatives, and whether there is a paediatric or neonatal exception.
The CLSI blood culture guideline is cited as the 2007 approved guideline. Please confirm this is the edition in force at your institution, or supply the current one.

slides.title: Blood Culture Collection and Nursing Care
slides.designRationale: Cover for the second section. The anchor image moves from the laboratory to the bedside, signalling the shift from understanding the test to performing it.

props.alt: Nurse performing venipuncture with a butterfly set, sharps tray in frame

slides.title: Learning objectives
slides.designRationale: The module objectives this section teaches, revealed one per narration line.

props.intro: By the end of this module, you will be able to:

items.text: Perform blood culture collection using aseptic technique
Prevent contamination and maintain specimen quality
Interpret blood culture results to distinguish true infection from contamination
Describe the nursing responsibilities, documentation and quality standards in blood culture sampling

props.text: This is the second of 2 sections. In this section, you will learn the nineteen-step collection procedure, how contamination happens and how to prevent it, how results are interpreted, and what the nurse is accountable for.

slides.title: The procedure in five stages
slides.designRationale: The source spreads nineteen numbered steps across five slides of dense bullets. Grouped into five stages the sequence becomes five things to remember, and any step can be placed inside one of them. The stage list stays on screen; only the detail expands.

props.text: Click each stage to see the steps it contains.

interaction.instruction: Click each stage to see the steps it contains.
interaction.buildAs: slide layers on this slide, not separate slides

layers.label: 1 - Before you start
lines: Verify the physician's order: number of sets, collection sites, timing in relation to antibiotics. Identify the patient with two identifiers. Explain the purpose, the brief discomfort and the need to stay still.

layers.label: 2 - Prepare
lines: Perform hand hygiene. Check bottle expiry, seal integrity, labels and request form. Disinfect the rubber septa with 70% alcohol and let them dry. Select a peripheral vein such as the median cubital.

layers.label: 3 - Antisepsis and access
lines: Apply the tourniquet and palpate the vein, releasing it temporarily if needed. Disinfect the skin with chlorhexidine and let it dry completely. Put on sterile gloves. Re-apply the tourniquet without touching the cleaned site.

layers.label: 4 - Draw and inoculate
lines: Perform venipuncture and collect the recommended volume. Inoculate the bottles in the right order for your device. Invert each bottle several times to mix blood with the culture medium.

layers.label: 5 - Finish
lines: Label at the bedside. Apply pressure and a dressing. Discard sharps immediately without recapping. Complete documentation. Send to the laboratory straight away.

embeddedStates.heading: What each stage requires
embeddedStates.designRationale: The expanded state of the stepper. Every one of the nineteen source steps is carried here in order, with the elaboration moved to the narration so no panel becomes a paragraph.

props.alt: Prepared blood culture tray: bottles, butterfly set, antiseptic swabs, gloves

slides.title: Check before you draw
slides.designRationale: Four checks that happen in the thirty seconds before the needle goes in, pulled out of the procedure stepper because each one independently causes a rejected specimen. Short, equal, no order - icons.

items.label: Seal integrity - no leaks, no cracks
Septa disinfected with 70% alcohol and dry

props.text: An expired bottle is discarded, never used and never re-sterilised. It will not support microbial growth, whatever the seal looks like.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: Placed immediately after the pre-draw checks, where the distractors are all things a busy nurse might genuinely talk themselves into.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: While preparing for blood culture collection, the nurse notices that the blood culture bottle has an expired date. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Use the bottle if the seal is intact
Discard the bottle and obtain a new one
Collect the sample and transfer it later

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Expired blood culture bottles may not support microbial growth adequately and should never be used.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Expired blood culture bottles may not support microbial growth adequately and should never be used.

slides.title: Labelling at the bedside
slides.designRationale: A correctly labelled bottle is something the learner has to be able to look at and check. Its own image-focus slide rather than a bullet inside the procedure, because mislabelling is one of the four rejection criteria and the commonest identification error in the ward.

props.alt: Close view of a labelled blood culture bottle, handwritten label legible
props.searchTerms: labelled blood culture bottle specimen label

candidates.note: Specimen labelling close-ups - choose one where the label fields are readable

props.text: Label at the bedside, immediately, before you leave the patient. Labelling at the nursing station is how specimens get swapped.

slides.title: Transport and storage
slides.designRationale: Three rules, one of which is a hard prohibition. Chips carry the reasoning, and the prohibition is lifted into a warning because refrigerating a blood culture is an intuitive mistake that destroys the specimen.

cards.title: Send immediately
cards.body: Straight to the microbiology laboratory for prompt processing.

cards.title: Never refrigerate
cards.body: Low temperatures inhibit the growth of the organisms you are trying to detect.

cards.title: If delay is unavoidable
cards.body: Hold at room temperature until transport.

props.text: Do not refrigerate blood culture bottles. A refrigerated specimen can return a false negative on a patient who is genuinely septic.

slides.title: True pathogen or contamination?
slides.designRationale: The single judgement this module exists to support, and it is a contrast - so the two readings sit side by side with the discriminating features aligned. A list would let the learner remember the features without the comparison.

columns.title: Likely a true pathogen
columns.body: Growth in multiple bottles  ·  the same organism in more than one set  ·  findings consistent with the patient's clinical condition

columns.title: Possibly contamination
columns.body: Growth in a single bottle only  ·  a common skin organism  ·  patient clinically stable with no signs of systemic infection

props.alt: Microbiology report or culture plate showing bacterial growth
props.searchTerms: blood culture positive growth laboratory report

props.text: Neither pattern is proof on its own. Clinical correlation decides - which is why the number of sets and the quality of the draw matter so much.

slides.title: How contamination happens
slides.designRationale: Five failures, each one a thing the nurse did or did not do - icons so each lands separately and the learner can recognise their own habits. Separated from the organisms, because cause and consequence are two different lessons.

items.label: Touching the puncture site after cleaning
Collecting through an existing IV line

slides.title: What grows when it does
slides.designRationale: Four named organisms the learner should recognise on a report as probable skin flora. Chips rather than icons, because the name is the content and an icon would add nothing.

cards.title: Coagulase-negative staphylococci
cards.body: The commonest contaminant by a wide margin.

cards.title: Bacillus species
cards.body: Except Bacillus anthracis, which is always significant.

props.text: Bacillus anthracis is the exception - never dismiss it as a contaminant.

slides.title: The contamination rate
slides.designRationale: A single number with consequences attached. A definition slide gives the target the prominence it needs as a ward-level quality measure, with the costs listed beneath rather than competing with it.

terms.description: The accepted benchmark for blood culture contamination.
False-positive results  ·  unnecessary antibiotic use  ·  increased hospital costs  ·  prolonged hospital stay

props.text: A contaminated culture is not a harmless error - it puts a patient on antibiotics they do not need, for an infection they do not have.

slides.title: Common errors and how to prevent them
slides.designRationale: Error against prevention - two-dimensional, so the source table is kept as a table. A 'what it costs' column surfaces the consequence, which is what makes the prevention worth doing rather than a rule to follow.

props.text: Common errors and how to prevent them

rows: Fill to the volume markings on the bottle
Strict aseptic technique and full drying time
Label at the bedside, before leaving the patient

slides.title: Why the laboratory rejects a specimen
slides.designRationale: Five rejection criteria, flat and equal, each of which means the patient is re-bled. Icons, and its own slide rather than a line in the errors table, because this is the list the learner checks against before the bottles leave their hand.

props.text: Why the laboratory rejects a specimen
Every rejection means re-bleeding the patient and losing hours. Thirty seconds of checking before transport is the cheapest step in the whole procedure.

slides.title: Complications during collection
slides.designRationale: Five complications, no order, each short - icons. Kept as its own slide because four of them affect the patient and one affects the nurse, and both halves of that need to be visible.

props.alt: Nurse applying pressure to a venipuncture site with gauze after a draw

props.text: Needlestick injury is the one complication that happens to you. Discard sharps immediately into the container, and never recap a needle.

slides.title: What you are accountable for
slides.designRationale: Seven responsibilities spanning the whole procedure - icons so they read as a checklist the nurse can run against their own practice, which is exactly how the audit will assess them.

slides.title: What to record, and why
slides.designRationale: The source lists six fields with no reason attached, which makes documentation feel like paperwork. Paired with why each field matters it becomes clinical information the next person needs - items by attributes, so a table.

rows: Fixes the sample against the fever curve and the antibiotic timeline
Lets a positive catheter set be compared against a peripheral one
Tells the laboratory and the clinician how to read a single positive
The main determinant of yield, and the first thing questioned on a negative
Flags complications and informs the next draw
Whether a negative result can be trusted

slides.title: Quality indicators
slides.designRationale: Five indicators with a target attached to each - items by attributes, so a table rather than the source's flat list. The target is the part that makes an indicator usable, and the source left it in the narration.

rows: Before the first dose of antibiotics
At the bedside, all four fields complete

slides.title: The collection audit checklist
slides.designRationale: Seven observable behaviours an auditor watches for. Kept separate from the indicators slide because an indicator is a number reported monthly and an audit item is a thing someone watches you do - different artefacts, different use.

props.text: Audit yourself before someone else does - run this list in your head on the next draw you do.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: Framed as an audit observation, which is how the learner will actually encounter this standard - and each distractor is a real shortcut seen on wards.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: During a quality audit, which practice best demonstrates compliance with blood culture collection standards?

options.text: Labeling bottles after returning to the nursing station
Labeling the bottles immediately at the patient's bedside
Transporting specimens at the end of the shift

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Immediate bedside labelling minimises identification errors and is a key quality indicator for safe blood culture collection.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Immediate bedside labelling minimises identification errors and is a key quality indicator for safe blood culture collection.

slides.title: Let's summarise the key points
slides.designRationale: Recap of the whole module in the order it was taught, closing on the nurse's role because that is the behaviour the course exists to change.

points: Blood culture detects bloodstream infection and guides targeted antimicrobial therapy.
Collect before antibiotics wherever possible - but never delay treatment in suspected sepsis.
Two sets routinely, three for endocarditis; 8-10 mL per bottle in adults.
Peripheral venipuncture preferred; aerobic first with a butterfly, anaerobic first with a syringe.
Antisepsis must dry completely, and the site is never touched afterwards.
Label at the bedside, send immediately, never refrigerate.
A single bottle growing skin flora in a stable patient is probably contamination.
Nurses safeguard quality through technique, volume, labelling, documentation and audit.
